facts.text: Star Paul Naschy wrote this script under his real name, Jacinto Molina. He used the Naschy pseudonym only on screen, reportedly to help sell the film to English-language audiences.
Jack Taylor (Dr. Henry Jekyll) is an American who also supplied the English dubbed voice of Paul Naschy in Naschy's 1970s Spanish horror films.
Dr. Henry Jekyll answers a nosy party guest's question about his grandfather by pointing to A Midsummer Night's Dream, where a man turns into a donkey. Be careful what you wish for.
Shirley Corrigan, the English actress playing newlywed Justine, got her nickname "Shirleybelle" from Mother Teresa.
Title card time: this is the only movie where the Jekyll/Hyde characters and Paul Naschy's Wolf Man appear together.
Director León Klimovsky worked as a dentist for 15 years before becoming a filmmaker.
This was Paul Naschy's second film with director León Klimovsky, after their hit Werewolf Shadow (La noche de Walpurgis, 1970). It didn't match that film's box office.
Paul Naschy's lost second Daninsky film, The Nights of the Wolf Man (1968), is why this is called the sixth wolf movie. Naschy reportedly remembered only a week shooting in Paris for it.
Genre Grinder's review says director León Klimovsky gives the film a respectful imitation of Hammer directors Terence Fisher and Freddie Francis, on roughly half the budget.
Production ran November to December 1971, but the film didn't reach Spanish theaters until November 13, 1972.
José Marco, who plays honeymooner Imre Kosta, also appeared in the cult train-monster film Horror Express (1972).
Writer Doris V. Sutherland compared this modern-London werewolf tale to Hammer's Dracula A.D. 1972: classic monsters dropped into groovy 1970s Britain.
Transylvania was played by Spain. Locations included the Castillo de Guadamur near Toledo, plus Madrid, while London was shot on location in Soho, Piccadilly and Westminster.
Paul Naschy's voice was almost always dubbed in the Spanish versions of his films, often by professional dubbers José Guardiola or Simón Ramírez.
Title changes: Dr. Jekyll and the Wolfman in the U.S. (1973), Dr. Jekyll and the Werewolf in the UK, and Night of the Bloody Wolves in Germany (1974).

Paul Naschy's barrel chest came from weightlifting, and he was once a pro wrestler. He later became known as the "Spanish Lon Chaney" for playing the Wolfman, Frankenstein's monster, Dracula and more.
Luis Induni, who plays village gang leader Otvos, had over 200 film credits by 1972. Kitley's Krypt notes he returned for Paul Naschy's Night of the Howling Beast (1975).
Paul Naschy plays three roles: Count Waldemar Daninsky, the Wolf Man, and Mr. Hyde. Richard Scheib of Moria notes Waldemar doesn't show up until well into the film.
1972 was Paul Naschy's busiest year as a writer: he wrote and starred in no fewer than seven movies.
In the 1950s, before Paul Naschy was a horror star, he wrote Western dime novels under the pseudonym Jack Mills.
Unlike most Waldemar Daninsky films, this one never explains how the werewolf curse started, according to Kitley's Krypt. It just drops in with Waldemar already afflicted.
Two cuts were made: a clothed version for Spanish theaters, and an export version with added nudity for everyone else. Some prints, like the German one, have different nude inserts again.
Director León Klimovsky founded Argentina's first film club in 1929. He also directed the spaghetti western Raise Your Hands Dead Man (1971).
The poster reportedly shows a severed head drawn to look like Justine, because Uswika Bathory's actress, Elsa Zabala, wasn't considered photogenic enough for the artwork.
Spanish genre films of this era were shot without synced sound and dubbed later. Genre Grinder's review says Jack Taylor (Dr. Jekyll) seems to have spoken English on set.
Paul Naschy's later spy spoof Operation Mantis (1985) lost so much money that his production company Aconito Films went bankrupt.
Mirta Miller, who plays Jekyll's jealous assistant Sandra, was born in Buenos Aires. She has appeared in more than 65 films since 1961.
Famous bit: Waldemar turns into the Wolf Man inside a stalled clinic elevator with a young nurse. Wikipedia lists it among the film's unusual transformation scenes.
Jack Taylor (Dr. Jekyll) got his start with an uncredited bit in Cleopatra (1963) and was a regular in Jesús Franco's Euro-horror, including Count Dracula (1970).
Jack Taylor (Dr. Jekyll) later played in the gory slasher Pieces (1982) and Roman Polanski's The Ninth Gate (1999).
In a 2002 interview, Paul Naschy called crossover films like this one "monster cocktails," according to Genre Grinder's review.
Nitpick: Dr. Henry Jekyll and assistant Sandra operate on and inject Waldemar without wearing scrubs, while he lies partly undressed.
A heavily cut 72-minute version of the film circulates on budget multi-film packs, missing much of the nudity and violence found in the 88-minute Code Red DVD cut.
Despite the title, Jekyll never turns into Hyde: Waldemar does. Richard Scheib of Moria complained that the promised "vs" showdown never arrives.
Kitley's Krypt praised Paul Naschy's Mr. Hyde as one of the best since Fredric March won an Oscar for the 1932 Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde.
Bands About Movies' review said Paul Naschy's grinning, hairpiece-wearing Mr. Hyde looks more like Bugs Bunny in the 1955 cartoon Hyde and Hare than a classic screen Hyde.
Composer Antón García Abril mixes sparse, Blind Dead-style horror music with contemporary jazz for the London scenes, according to Mondo Esoterica's review.
London shoot: the film used real locations including Trafalgar Square, Piccadilly Circus, Soho and the Houses of Parliament with Big Ben.
Killer Horror Critic notes the film is basically two Waldemar Daninsky stories joined end to end: a Gothic Transylvania tale, then a modern London one.
Mondo Esoterica's reviewer described Jekyll's deathbed scene as one of the most dragged-out in movie history. Yes, he really does keep talking.
Continuity goof: Dr. Jekyll closes his eyes after his last words, then the cut to the close-up shows them open again.
Waldemar changes inside a packed Soho disco. Strobe lights and rapid full-moon shots sell the transformation, according to Mondo Esoterica's review.
The film's tagline: "To destroy the Monster, was to destroy the one she loved!! Could she? Could you?"
The next Waldemar Daninsky adventure was Curse of the Devil (El retorno de Walpurgis, 1973). The saga eventually ran to 12 films.
Richard Scheib of Moria gave the film two and a half stars out of five. He called the first half a "timewaster" but said the second half works.
Mondo Esoterica's review says Paul Naschy's sneering Mr. Hyde foreshadows his villain de Marnac in the 1973 film El espanto surge de la tumba (Horror Rises from the Tomb).
